docs.text: What is Basalo? Basalo is an international auxiliary language (IAL): a language created by a person or group of people in order to give people across the world a common, universal way of communicating with each other. These languages are often very simple—in terms of grammar, vocabulary, and even sounds—to help make the language as easy to learn as possible. Basalo, as an IAL, strives to represent three main tenets: to be simple and easy to learn, to use a vocabulary from all across the world, and to maintain cultural neutrality. Many international auxiliary languages that use words from languages worldwide will restrict their vocabulary to a specific set of languages: Lingwa de Planeta is based on 10 languages, Baseyu on 15, and Pandunia on 21, just to name a few. Basalo, however, has no restriction on what languages are represented; there are over 150 unique languages that Basalo has a word from! This gives Basalo the unique advantage of being able to represent all cultures, leveling the playing field between communities big and small. Here's a map showing just some of the languages Basalo already represents! Community and development Basalo has a dedicated community of learners and supporters in the official Discord server . In this server, people can learn and discuss Basalo, as well as suggest any changes or additions to the language. If you're interested in learning Basalo, or just want to check it out, anyone is free to join! Basalo is always growing and changing, and feedback is always appreciated.

docs.text: table { max-width: 66%; font-size: 100%; } Lesson 1 — Sounds and spelling Basalo's alphabet consists of 19 letters; 14 consonants and 5 vowels. Basalo uses the regular English alphabet, minus the letters h , j , q , r , v , x , and z . a, b, c, d, e, f, g, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, s, t, u, w, y Sounds The unique thing about Basalo is that its sounds are able to be pronounced a variety of ways. Most are pronounced the same as in English: p, t, k — like in p ay, t ake, k ing b, d, g — like in b an, d arn, g ame f — like in f amous m, n — like in m orning, n oon y — like in y ear a — like in f a ther i — like in t ee th u — like in b oo n e — like in b e d o — like in o wn It's important to never reduce vowel sounds in Basalo. In English, we reduce vowels all the time, like in a bout , tak e n , d i vide , acti o n , and s u pport . In Basalo, vowels can never be reduced like this—vowels always make the same sound regardless of where they are. A couple are pronounced sometimes like in English, but with some variations: s — like in s ip or z ip w — like in w ine or v ine l — like in l ake or r ake And the last one is pronounced much differently than in English: c — like in ch ump or j ump Some words have two vowels right next to each other, or a vowel at the very beginning. You'll often hear either a small stop between the vowels (like in uh - oh ) or a "h" sound between the vowels when these words are pronounced. Examples We'll look at a few words in Basalo and how to pronounce them: Basalo Meaning Pronunciation un one oon owi hole oh-wee, oh-vee cek dot check musik music moo-seek, moo-zeek pim five peem oyla think oy-lah kafe coffee kah-feh yati speak yah-tee nui nose noo-ee, noo-hee Capitalization and punctuation In Basalo, there is no capitalization needed at all. Beyond that, Basalo uses most basic punctuation, like question marks, excalamtion points, periods, and commas. imut sin! — "Good to see you!" yo sin e amal mea ta, o can! — "Meet my friend, John!" me yo kan e lel cu? — "Can I have it?"

docs.text: table { max-width: 80%; font-size: 100%; } Lesson 2 — How to make a sentence Basalo sentences are very free in the order that words go in. However, there are a few rules: The person doing an action, or the subject , has a before it, The person experiencing an action, or the object , has a preposition before it (usually e ), And modifying words (adjectives, adverbs) will always come after what they modify. If a or e is the first word of a sentence, it should be dropped! Statements With these rules, let's see a few example sentences: Basalo English me yo kan e fon la naya! I have a new phone! yo dolna a le He is running. wangu a salam yo ide. The man is going to the market. ca la enyum yo esa a me. I'm drinking some hot tea. You'll notice that the verbs in these sentences all have yo before them. This word describes an action that's unfinished or still happening, and always goes directly before the verb. me yo sin e salam. — I see a person. / I'm seeing a person. me a les yo ogop cu? — Can they help me? yo esa a mes e kafe! — We're drinking some coffee! You'll also see the word la in the phrases fon la naya and ca la enyum . This word goes right before any adjectives that modify a noun or noun phrase. yay la imut - a good performance pole la ik pasa - a small, peaceful field gidas lua la aga - two big houses Questions Yes-no questions are made by putting the question particle cu at the end of a sentence; sort of like a spoken question mark. le yo kan e kitap. — He has a book. le yo kan e kitap cu? — Does he have a book (yes or no)? Content questions (questions about "who", "what", "where", etc.) are made by putting the quetion particle ki at the end of a sentence. yo ista a me e bananas! - I like bananas! yo ista a te e kel ki? - What do you like? (You like what?) Negatives In general, you can make a sentence negative by putting ma right after the verb: aman yo nalu. — The water is rippling. aman yo nalu ma. — The water is not rippling. You can negate a specific word in a sentence by putting ma after it. inaki ma yo esa e owoce. — The dog isn't eating the fruit. inaki yo esa e owoce ma. — The dog isn't eating the fruit . Wait, how do you say "the" and "a"? You don't! Or, more precisely, there's no dedicated word for either of these. If you want to refer to one thing, you could use un , meaning "one": mama — the parent, a parent mama un — one parent And if you want to refer to some specific object, you could use lel , which means "this" or "that". We'll become more acquainted with words related to lel in Lesson 5, as it's one of the doskamolas : kin — the plant, a plant kin lel — that specific plant Remember, don't get confused with the word la ; it's just there to separate adjectives from nouns: oto la naya — a new car, the new car umal la idaman — a red apple, the red apple Using lel versus le Both lel and le are very versatile words which we'll see a lot in the coming lessons. In short, le means "he" or "she", while lel can mean "this" or "that". le yo meti e kitap lel. — He's putting down that book. yo sin a te e le cu? — Do you guys see her? When we use lel after a noun earlier in a sentence, we can refer to that whole noun by just using lel , like so: salam lel , lel e kitap meya yo kan cu? — That guy , does he have my book? te e yoku lel la naya yo sin? lel yo e kul aga. — Are you seeing that new game ? It 's super cool. Some words to start with Now that we know how to put sentences together, here's a few words you can play around with: me , te , le — I/me, you, he/she mes , tes , les — we/us, you all, they lel — this, that salam — person, man, woman mama — parent, mother, father kitap — to read; book sin — to see, look at esa — to eat, to drink; food, beverage yati — to speak, talk; speech

docs.text: table { max-width: 100%; font-size: 100%; } Work in progress! Lesson 3 — Making new words Basalo's vocabulary has many terms made up of multiple words. While sometimes these compound words are made of two full words, most of the time they're made up of one full word and one or more affixes, which in Basalo are called kesekumolas . There's quite a bit, but don't worry! We won't need to learn them all now, and you'll come to recognize them in words with time. For now, let's look at some of the most useful ones: kesekumol Meaning Examples -(a)lo tool, item naso "to write" → nasolo "pencil, pen" -(a)pi becoming, changing al "knowledge" → alapi "to learn" -(a)tel do-er, occupation fas "to create" → fasatel "creator" -(i)gi causing, result iso "equal" → isogi "to balance" -(n)ik little, small siku "ice" → sikunik "snow"
